Cancer patients face treatment delays as SHA approval system falters, KENCO warns
items.description: Cancer patients across Kenya are facing interruptions in treatment, rising medical expenses and delays in accessing essential drugs following changes in the Social Health Authority (SHA) approval and pricing arrangements, the Kenyan Network of Cancer Organizations (KENCO) has warned.
content: Cancer patients across Kenya are facing interruptions in treatment, rising medical expenses and delays in accessing essential drugs following changes in the Social Health Authority (SHA) approval and pricing arrangements, the Kenyan Network of Cancer Organizations (KENCO) has warned.

The organization says patients seeking cancer treatment in both public and private hospitals are being turned away, forced to pay out of pocket for services covered by SHA or in some cases, switch medication because of reductions in approved drug limits.

Speaking to the press on Thursday, KENCO Advocacy Sub-committee Chairperson Prisca Githuka said the new arrangements had created uncertainty among cancer patients, particularly those already undergoing treatment.

Githuka said although KENCO welcomed the government’s decision to increase the oncology benefit by more than 40 per cent, the improvements would mean little if patients could not access treatment when they needed it.

“A benefit that cannot be accessed on the day of treatment is no benefit at all. Cancer patients are going days without treatment, being turned away from health facilities and paying out of pocket for care that SHA is supposed to cover,” she said.
She noted that the challenges had emerged following recent changes in approval procedures and pricing of cancer treatment, with complaints reported in several counties.

KENCO states that the revised arrangements were introduced without adequate preparation or transitional safeguards, exposing patients already receiving chemotherapy, hormonal therapy and other specialized cancer treatments to unnecessary interruptions.
Githuka said patients should not be forced to change medication or interrupt prescribed treatment because of administrative changes.

“For patients already undergoing treatment, any interruption arising from new approval requirements or pricing discrepancies poses a direct clinical risk and cannot be treated as a mere administrative inconvenience,” she said.

The concerns come despite SHA maintaining that the oncology benefit remains at Sh800,000, comprising Sh400,000 under the Social Health Insurance Fund (SHIF) and another Sh400,000 under the Emergency, Chronic and Critical Illness Fund (ECCIF).
KENCO said the changes were intended to standardize treatment costs, align services with national cancer treatment guidelines and prevent patients from exhausting their benefits prematurely.
However, the organization maintained that the implementation had created barriers that were undermining access to essential services.
Among the concerns raised are sudden reductions in approved drug limits, increased treatment costs, exclusion of specialized diagnostic tests and scans, and delays in digital authorisation.
One breast cancer patient reportedly said SHA had reduced the approved limit for a particular drug, forcing her to switch medication after completing six cycles of treatment.
The organization also raised concerns over discrepancies between approved amounts, prices reflected on the SHA portal and actual costs charged by health facilities.

The organization also expressed concern over the reported failure of the SHA digital authorisation system in several health facilities, warning that patients were being forced to make private payments or postpone treatment when the platform was unavailable.

KENCO said the rule inconvenienced patients whose prescribed medication could not be fully supplied at one hospital, forcing them to wait until the following day to obtain the remaining drugs from another facility.
Githuka called on the Ministry of Health and SHA to introduce urgent measures to ensure patients already undergoing treatment were protected from the effects of the new arrangements.

She proposed that the previous and revised systems operate concurrently until the new procedures are fully stabilized, adding that patients should be allowed to access medication from a second facility on the same day where the first hospital could not meet their prescriptions.
KENCO also wants SHA to establish clear timelines for approving cancer treatment, including same-day authorisation for urgent cases and an escalation mechanism for delayed applications.
Githuka said cancer patient organisations should also be involved in decisions affecting the financing and delivery of cancer care.

Okoth Obado: Ex-Kenyan governor jailed for 25 years for killing pregnant girlfriend
items.description: The pregnant student was murdered after leaving a hotel with a journalist she had contacted to discuss her affair with the governor.
content: A former Kenyan governor has been jailed for 25 years for the murder of a university student who was seven months pregnant with his child.
The High Court on Friday sentenced Zacharia Okoth Obado, the former governor of Migori County, along with two former aides, over the 2018 killing of Sharon Belyne Otieno.
The investigation established that an "intimate relationship" had existed between Obado and Otieno, which "subsequently led to a pregnancy with the deceased that the governor was unhappy about".
Both Obado and Otieno's legal teams said they would appeal against the sentence.
His former personal assistant, Michael Oyamo, was also sentenced to 25 years in prison, while former county clerk Caspal Ojwang' Obiero received an 18-year sentence.
The court found that Obado had provided the motive and financial resources for the murder, while Oyamo coordinated its execution and Obiero provided logistical support and helped conceal the crime.
Judge Cecilia Githua said Obado's absence from Migori at the time of the killing did not absolve him of responsibility.
She rejected the prosecution's request for the death penalty, as well as Obado's plea for a non-custodial sentence.
Otieno, 26, was killed between 3 and 4 September 2018 after leaving a hotel in Rongo, south-western Kenya, with journalist Barrack Oduor.
She had contacted Oduor to discuss her relationship with the then-governor. The two were abducted shortly afterwards.
Oduor managed to escape by jumping out of a moving vehicle. His account of the abduction became a crucial lead in the investigation.
Otieno's body was later found near Kodera Forest.
A post-mortem examination found that she had died from strangulation and excessive bleeding caused by multiple stab wounds.
The court also established that Obado was the biological father of her unborn child.
Obado and his co-accused were convicted of murder on 23 July 2026, following a lengthy trial in which prosecutors called 42 witnesses and presented 81 exhibits.
On Friday, the court declined to award compensation to Otieno's family, saying there was insufficient evidence to establish the financial losses they had claimed.
Before sentencing, Otieno's mother had appealed to the judge not to send Obado to prison, saying his imprisonment would amount to "another death in the family".
She urged the court to consider a non-custodial sentence, arguing that Otieno's three children, from different relationships, needed his support.
But the judge said the family's circumstances could not override the court's responsibility to impose an appropriate punishment.
Otieno's family, through their lawyer Antony Opondo, told Kenya's Daily Nation that they would file an appeal seeking Obado's acquittal.
Otieno's murder sparked protests and renewed public debate about violence against women in Kenya.
A national survey found that at least 34% of women had experienced physical violence in 2022.
The case has also drawn attention because it is rare for such senior political figures to face public criminal trials in Kenya.
Obado served two terms as governor of Migori County in western Kenya, switching allegiance between a smaller political party and the region's dominant opposition movement.
He later backed President William Ruto and formally joined his ruling party in 2023, becoming a regional organiser.

Rwanda approves Samuel Nganga as World Bank manager
items.description: Kenyan professional Samuel Kamau Nganga has landed a prestigious international appointment after Rwanda's Cabinet approved him as the new World Bank Group
content: Kenyan professional Samuel Kamau Nganga has landed a prestigious international appointment after Rwanda’s Cabinet approved him as the new World Bank Group Country Manager for Rwanda, placing him at the heart of the institution’s development and investment partnership with the East African nation.

The appointment, announced following a Cabinet meeting on Thursday, November 26, 2026, represents a significant career milestone for Nganga, whose professional journey at the World Bank Group spans nearly two decades.
He takes over from Sahr Kpundeh, who held the position from September 2023 until August 31, 2026.

Nganga’s appointment is particularly significant because he will become the first World Bank Group Country Manager in Rwanda to oversee all four institutions operating under the World Bank Group through a unified leadership structure.

The four institutions are the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD), International Development Association (IDA), International Finance Corporation (IFC) and Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (MIGA).
This consolidated arrangement is expected to strengthen coordination between development financing, private-sector investment, technical support and investment-risk guarantees.
Equity Group, ZEP-RE sign deal to widen farm finance access

In his new position, Nganga will lead the World Bank Group’s engagement with the Rwandan government and private sector, while supervising the formulation and implementation of programmes aligned with the country’s development priorities.

His mandate will place particular emphasis on employment creation, poverty reduction, private-sector expansion and shared economic prosperity. Nganga’s rise to the prestigious position follows an impressive career trajectory within the World Bank Group.

The Kenyan national joined the institution in 2007 through its Sub-Saharan Africa Department and progressively assumed increasingly senior responsibilities across different geographical regions and economic sectors.

He previously served as Regional Head of Operations for the International Finance Corporation across Africa. Immediately before his latest appointment, he was Manager of the IFC’s Manufacturing, Agribusiness and Services Africa department. In that capacity, he supervised investment and advisory programmes designed to stimulate private-sector growth across East and Southern Africa.

His professional expertise extends across manufacturing, agribusiness, consumer services, renewable energy, digital financial services, healthcare, education and financing for small and medium-sized enterprises. The breadth of his experience places him in a strategic position to connect development financing with practical economic opportunities.

Nganga assumes office as Rwanda and the World Bank Group prepare a new Country Partnership Framework covering 2027 to 2035. The framework will provide the strategic blueprint for the institution’s investments, technical assistance and advisory services in Rwanda over the next eight years.

His leadership will therefore be central to determining how World Bank resources and expertise support Rwanda’s economic transformation, strengthen businesses, expand employment opportunities and improve the livelihoods of citizens.

items.title: Martha Karua: Kenya’s new dawn starts now
items.description: PLP leader Martha Karua thanked Kenyans for their support after her 27 November 2026 presidential declaration, calling for unity ahead of the 2027 General Election
content: The PLP leader thanks her supporters after her presidential declaration, calling on Kenyans to build a country worthy of their children’s future.

Martha Karua, leader of the People’s Liberation Party, has thanked Kenyans for their warmth and encouragement following her presidential declaration on Friday, 27 November 2026, calling the outpouring of support a sign of how much the country shares in common despite its divisions.

Speaking after the event, Karua addressed those who had travelled from across Kenya to witness the declaration. “To everyone who came, who stood with us, who travelled from near and far, and who gave their time, energy and heart to make today possible, thank you,” she said.

Her message struck a deliberately unifying tone at the opening of what is expected to be a fiercely contested road to the August 2027 General Election. “I know that the road ahead will not be easy, but I also know that we have so much more in common than what divides us,” she added.

At the heart of her post-declaration remarks was a vision of Kenya defined by dignity, institutional integrity and opportunity. “I believe in a Kenya where every citizen has dignity, where hard work opens doors, and where our children can look to the future with confidence.”
That Kenya, she said, is worth building together.

items.title: Martha Karua declares 2027 presidential bid
items.description: Martha Karua, People's Liberation Party leader, formally declared her 2027 Kenya presidential candidacy on 27 November 2026 in Nairobi, outlining a detailed policy platform.
content: People’s Liberation Party leader Martha Karua has formally entered the 2027 presidential race, anchoring her campaign on economic accountability, healthcare, education and the restoration of constitutional order.

Martha Karua, leader of the People’s Liberation Party, on Friday declared her candidature for the presidency of the Republic of Kenya in the 2027 General Election, delivering a sweeping policy address in Nairobi that placed women at the centre of her campaign coalition while extending her appeal to every Kenyan household struggling under the weight of a deepening economic and governance crisis.

The declaration, made on Friday, 27 November 2026, was framed not as a moment of personal ambition but as a response to what Karua described as a profound crisis of leadership and a dangerous deficit of public trust — one that she argued was being felt in markets, hospitals, schools and homes across the country.

“Today, our country is facing a profound crisis of leadership and a deep deficit of public trust,” she told those gathered. “This crisis affects every household. It hurts our children, our families, our men and women, and threatens our collective future.”

Karua opened her address with a direct appeal to women, whom she identified as her primary constituency — not because she intended to exclude others, but because she said she understood, from lived experience, the burdens women carry as caregivers, providers and community anchors. The vision she set out, however, was explicitly national in scope: a government that serves every Kenyan regardless of gender, region or political affiliation.

Her economic platform is built around a central image — a mother at a market stall with a thousand shillings, buying essentials, calculating the fare home and quietly returning the sugar to the shelf. It is, Karua argued, the most honest description of what macroeconomic failure actually looks like at household level, and it is the standard against which she intends to hold herself accountable.
“Public money must serve the public,” she said. “Every shilling must count.”

On the economy, Karua committed to fair and responsible taxation that does not crush households or stifle enterprise, prompt payment of suppliers and pending bills, a crackdown on corruption and wastage, and a sharp prioritisation of essential services — healthcare, education, infrastructure and food security — over what she characterised as unnecessary government expenditure. For farmers, she cited the specific example of potato growers selling below the cost of production on harvest day, their bargaining power gone, their next planting season in jeopardy. Her government, she said, would work with county governments and farmers’ organisations to improve access to quality inputs, storage, irrigation and reliable markets, while pushing for greater local value addition across agricultural commodities including tea, coffee and horticulture.

For young people, the commitment is to close the gap between training and employment through expanded apprenticeships and structured partnerships between technical institutions and private-sector employers. For small businesses and traders, it is predictable taxation, transparent licensing and a government that actually pays its bills on time.

The transparency pillar of her platform is specific and verifiable. She pledged that if ten million shillings were allocated to build a road in any ward in Kenya, any citizen would be able to establish how much was approved, who received the contract, what was delivered, how much was paid and who signed off on the work — through digital platforms and accessible public noticeboards. The same accountability framework, she said, would apply to hospitals, schools, water projects and every publicly funded programme.

On healthcare, Karua was direct: no parent should take a sick child to a public hospital and return home with a prescription they cannot afford to fill, and no family should lose a loved one because essential medicines are unavailable. She committed to progressively realising universal healthcare free at the point of treatment, backed by adequate budgetary allocations, timely payments to health facilities and fair remuneration for health workers. On education, she committed to universal free public education, progressively extended from pre-primary through to university, with a funded implementation plan and a review of the competency-based curriculum in genuine consultation with teachers and parents.

The human rights section of her declaration was among its most pointed. Karua committed to strengthening the institutional response to domestic violence, sexual abuse and femicide, demanding prompt investigations, evidence handling, survivor protection and accountability for perpetrators. She pledged full implementation of the constitutional two-thirds gender principle in government appointments. And she was unequivocal on security: there would be no tolerance for abductions, extrajudicial killings or enforced disappearances under her administration. Security agencies, she stated plainly, exist to protect citizens, not to terrorise them.

On devolution, she committed to equitable, predictable and timely disbursement of funds to county governments, published transfer schedules, and an active strengthening of the Equalisation Fund to address persistent service inequalities. On the Constitution, she was equally plain — court orders would be obeyed, parliamentary oversight would be respected without interference, and the rule of law would apply equally to everyone, including those occupying the highest offices in the land.

In a move designed to signal that her accountability commitments are immediate rather than aspirational, Karua outlined four specific deliverables for her first 100 days in office: a published statement of national debt and pending bills; a register of stalled national projects showing amounts spent and work outstanding; a funded timetable for settling arrears owed to hospitals and schools; and the launch of project-level expenditure records accessible to ordinary citizens. On the hundredth day, she said, she would report publicly on progress against each commitment, name who was responsible for delays and state when outstanding work would be completed.

Karua has previously served as a Member of Parliament for Gichugu constituency, as Minister for Justice and Constitutional Affairs under President Mwai Kibaki, and as running mate to Raila Odinga in the 2022 presidential election. She resigned from the Ministry of Justice on principle — a decision she referenced in her declaration as formative to her understanding of what genuine public accountability requires.

Her entry into the 2027 presidential race reorders the emerging field and adds a voice with an unusually detailed — and testable — policy platform to what has, until now, been a contest defined more by political realignment than by programmatic substance.

For the mother quietly returning the sugar to the shelf at the market stall, the question Karua posed is direct: does the person asking for your vote manage public money with the same discipline, care and sacrifice that you apply to yours?

items.title: Martha Karua biography: Career, politics and 2027 role
items.description: Explore Martha Karua’s biography, legal career, tenure as Justice Minister, People’s Liberation Party leadership, and 2027 presidential election strategy.
content: Former Justice Minister rebrands party to People’s Liberation Party and declares 2027 presidential bid while anchoring United Opposition unity talks ahead of the General Election

Martha Wangari Karua, Senior Counsel, former Cabinet Minister, and Party Leader of the People’s Liberation Party (PLP), has formally entered the race for State House ahead of the August 10, 2027 General Election. Born on September 22, 1957, in Kimunye village, Gichugu Constituency, Kirinyaga County, Karua has spent more than four decades in public life spanning the judiciary, private legal practice, parliamentary representation, ministerial portfolios, regional human rights advocacy, and national opposition leadership.

Karua began her primary education at Mugumo Primary School before attending Kabare Girls Boarding School and St. Michael’s Boarding School in Kerugoya. She pursued her secondary education at Kiburia Girls Secondary School, Ngiriambu Girls’ Secondary School, and Karoti Girls’ Secondary School, where she sat her East African School Certificate. She completed her Advanced Level studies at Nairobi Girls’ Secondary School before enrolling at the University of Nairobi, graduating with a Bachelor of Laws degree in 1980. In 1981, she earned a Postgraduate Diploma in Legal Practice from the Kenya School of Law and was admitted to the Roll of Advocates of the High Court of Kenya. She later attained a Master of Business Administration from the United States International University–Africa (USIU-Africa) to strengthen her executive and governance credentials.

Her professional career began on the bench in 1981 when she joined the judiciary as a magistrate, rising to the rank of Senior Resident Magistrate before leaving public judicial service in 1987. She subsequently established Martha Karua & Company Advocates, operating a private legal practice in Nairobi from 1987 to 2002. During the height of single-party rule under President Daniel arap Moi, Karua emerged as a prominent constitutional and human rights litigator, representing political detainees, journalists, and pro-democracy activists. Her work alongside the “Young Turks” and women’s rights groups during the push for multi-party democracy earned her national recognition, including being named Jurist of the Year by the International Commission of Jurists (Kenya Section) in 1999.

Karua’s elective political career commenced in the historic 1992 multi-party General Election when she won the Gichugu Constituency parliamentary seat on a Democratic Party (DP) ticket. She retained the seat across four consecutive terms, serving continuously in the National Assembly for two decades until 2013. Following the National Rainbow Coalition (NARC) victory in 2002, President Mwai Kibaki appointed her Minister for Water Resources Management and Development, where she spearheaded sweeping reforms in water governance and service delivery. In 2005, she was appointed Minister for Justice, National Cohesion and Constitutional Affairs, a portfolio she retained in the Grand Coalition Cabinet formed after the contested 2007 election.

During her tenure at the Justice Ministry, Karua was a central figure in legislative and institutional reform initiatives, though she resigned from Cabinet in April 2009, citing frustrations over executive interference and the appointment of judges without her consultation. Having assumed leadership of NARC–Kenya in 2008, she contested the presidency for the first time in 2013, later running for the Kirinyaga gubernatorial seat in 2017. In May 2022, she made political history when former Prime Minister Raila Odinga selected her as his running mate under the Azimio la Umoja–One Kenya Coalition, becoming the first woman nominated as deputy presidential candidate on a major Kenyan ticket.

Ahead of the 2027 election cycle, Karua has reshaped her political vehicle and regional profile. In early 2025, she officially rebranded NARC–Kenya into the People’s Liberation Party (PLP), launching grassroots mobilisation drives across the country and pledging to serve a single five-year term if elected to demystify executive power. Beyond domestic politics, she has remained active in East African legal advocacy, notably serving as lead counsel for detained Ugandan opposition figure Dr. Kizza Besigye—a role that saw her denied entry and deported from Uganda in June 2026.

On November 27, 2026, Karua officially launched her second presidential bid in Nairobi under the banner “Simama na Martha”. Her campaign platform centres on seven pillars: economic reforms and auditing public debt, accountable leadership, affordable healthcare, universal free public education, protection of human rights, strengthening independent institutions, and safeguarding devolution. While positioning herself as a reformist contender to challenge President William Ruto, Karua remains a key principal within the United Opposition alongside leaders such as Kalonzo Musyoka, Rigathi Gachagua, and Eugene Wamalwa, maintaining that she will back a single coalition flag bearer selected through a transparent mechanism to unseat the Kenya Kwanza administration.

items.title: Munyua Waiyaki: The son of Njoro eyeing Nakuru’s top seat
items.description: Njoro-born Jubilee aspirant Munyua Waiyaki is building his 2027 Nakuru gubernatorial bid on deep community roots and a development agenda for the county.
content: Njoro-born aspirant Munyua Waiyaki is building his gubernatorial bid on deep community roots, agricultural priorities and a vision for inclusive development across Nakuru County.

Munyua Waiyaki, the Jubilee Party aspirant seeking the Nakuru gubernatorial seat, is staking his political future on something that cannot be borrowed or manufactured — the lived experience of growing up in Njoro, one of Nakuru County’s most agriculturally significant areas, and the deep community ties that come with it.

For Waiyaki, the connection to Nakuru is not a campaign construct. It is personal, rooted in childhood, shaped by the rhythms of rural life and reinforced by decades spent among the farming families, young people and ordinary households whose daily realities form the backbone of the county’s social and economic fabric.

He was born and raised in Njoro, Nakuru County — a place he identifies not simply as his constituency of interest but as home, in every meaningful sense of the word. That identity sits at the heart of his emerging political message as Kenya moves steadily towards the 2027 General Election.

His pitch to voters is disarmingly direct: Nakuru deserves leadership that knows its people from the inside, not from campaign briefings. A governor who grew up here, he argues, carries a different kind of knowledge — one forged through personal experience rather than political calculation.

Waiyaki identifies closely with the farming communities that form the economic foundation of much of Nakuru County. For the smallholder farmers of Njoro and Molo, the challenges are longstanding and familiar — unreliable market access, rising cost of farm inputs, deteriorating rural road networks and returns that rarely reflect the effort invested. Agriculture in Nakuru supports thousands of households, underpins local food security and contributes significantly to the county’s economic output. Yet it remains chronically underfunded and poorly served by county infrastructure.

For Waiyaki, addressing these failures is not a policy position adopted for the campaign trail. It is, he says, an obligation shaped by his own upbringing in a farming community and by his understanding of how much rural livelihoods depend on decisions made in county government.

Beyond agriculture, he speaks with evident concern about the aspirations of young people across Nakuru — those who have invested in education and technical training but continue to find the doors to meaningful employment firmly shut. His argument here is substantive: leadership must move beyond political promises and focus on building the conditions in which young people can establish enterprises, access skills development programmes, attract investment and participate fully in the economy.

The concern for families is equally practical. Across Nakuru County, reliable water supply, accessible healthcare facilities, quality schools, functional roads and improved living standards remain aspirations rather than guaranteed realities for many households. Waiyaki is clear that effective county leadership must begin with an honest reckoning with these everyday pressures and a commitment to delivering practical, measurable improvements.

His insistence on the significance of his Njoro roots, however, is not simply a sentimental appeal. It is a deliberate political argument — that a leader’s personal history matters, that growing up within a community provides insight that cannot be replicated through consultations or community visits, and that voters have legitimate reasons to consider the depth of a candidate’s connection to the people they seek to serve.

His message is also directed at the full breadth of the Nakuru County electorate. The county is diverse — encompassing the agricultural zones of Njoro and Molo, the pastoral and mixed farming areas of Subukia, the trading centres of Naivasha, and the urban commercial and industrial activity of Nakuru City, one of Kenya’s fastest-growing urban centres. Nakuru is also among Kenya’s economically significant counties, with considerable opportunities in agriculture, trade, tourism, manufacturing, education and real estate. Its continued development requires leadership capable of connecting these sectors, reducing inequality between rural and urban areas, and ensuring that growth reaches communities across the entire county.

The challenge Waiyaki faces, as his candidacy takes shape, is precisely that translation — from a compelling personal narrative and genuine grassroots connection into a credible, countywide development agenda that addresses the practical concerns of a large and varied electorate.

He is aware of this. His campaign positioning, while anchored firmly in his Njoro identity, reaches beyond it. He frames himself not merely as a candidate for one part of the county but as someone whose roots give him the foundation to serve all of Nakuru’s residents with understanding, accountability and commitment. He has spoken directly about the need for inclusive leadership that recognises the needs of farmers, businesspeople, workers, young people, women, professionals and vulnerable households in equal measure.

His association with the Jubilee Party places his candidacy within the broader national political realignment now well underway ahead of 2027, as parties and aspirants across Kenya position for the next electoral contest. How that affiliation plays in Nakuru, a county with complex and shifting political loyalties, will be among the factors that determine whether Waiyaki’s personal appeal translates into a winning coalition.

For now, he is focused on making the case to Nakuru voters — particularly those in Njoro and the surrounding agricultural belt — that homegrown leadership represents a genuine opportunity to strengthen representation, improve service delivery and build a county government that understands its people because it was shaped by them.
Munyua Waiyaki’s message, stripped to its essence, is straightforward: Nakuru’s future is best built by someone who grew up carrying it.

Transport CS Chirchir Announces Tougher Vehicle Inspection, Enforcement on Kenyan Roads
items.description: Kenya plans automated vehicle inspections and digital enforcement under a KSh 30bn action plan targeting a 30% fall in road deaths over five years in Kenya.
content: PAY ATTENTION: TUKO is in WhatsApp Channels now! Subscribe and read news in your favourite messenger.

Transport Cabinet Secretary Davis Chirchir has outlined plans to overhaul motor vehicle inspections in Kenya, introducing automated testing facilities and digital systems as part of a broader push to make roads safer across the country.
Chirchir made the announcement on Thursday, 26 November, at the Africa Road Safety Conference, which was convened by KCB Group and the Global Road Safety Partnership.

The CS said the government aimed to cut road fatalities by more than 30% over the next five years, with a longer-term goal of reducing deaths and injuries by at least 50% by 2030. He reaffirmed the Ministry of Roads and Transport's commitment to achieving those targets through a range of interventions.

He added that enforcement on the roads would be intensified, with authorities cracking down on speeding, drunk driving, dangerous overtaking, overloading and reckless driving. Technology will play a central role in that effort.
Chirchir also announced the establishment of the Kenya Road Assessment Programme (KenRAP), designed to identify high-risk sections of road and prioritise remedial work at accident blackspots.

On public transport, he said operator accountability was being strengthened alongside professional driver training. More than 4,000 public transport personnel and drivers completed training in the past three months, according to the CS.
All these measures fall under the KSh 30 billion Road Safety Action Plan covering 2024 to 2028, which also addresses motorcycle safety and improved enforcement capacity.
ENA Coach issues reminder notice to mums travelling with minors

The announcement arrives against a contentious backdrop. Earlier this year, the National Transport and Safety Authority (NTSA) had proposed rules requiring private vehicles older than four years to undergo annual inspections covering brakes, tyres, steering systems and other safety-critical components.

In July, however, the Senate annulled those rules, raising concerns that the implementation window was too short and that existing inspection facilities were insufficient to handle the volume of private vehicles. Senators also warned that the shortage of inspection centres could leave motorists vulnerable to harassment by enforcement officers.

Chirchir's latest statements suggest the government is pressing ahead with its road safety agenda despite that legislative setback, with a greater emphasis on automated infrastructure to address the capacity concerns that derailed the earlier proposals.

items.title: Kenya Airways Issues Early Warning as Fuel Costs Surge, Earnings Decline
items.description: Kenya Airways warns 2026 earnings could fall at least 25% as fuel costs reach half of operating expenses, following a KSh 17.2bn loss in 2025 amid fuel surge.
content: Search option is now available at TUKO! Feel free to search the content on topics/people you enjoy reading about in the top right corner ;)

Kenya Airways has issued a formal profit warning to investors, disclosing that its earnings for the financial year ending 31 December 2026 are expected to drop by at least 25% compared to 2025 figures.

The announcement, signed by Board Chairman Kiprono Kittony on 26 November 2026, cited soaring fuel costs linked to the ongoing Middle East conflict and widespread supply chain disruptions as the primary drivers of the anticipated decline.
The warning was issued in line with Kenya's Capital Markets (Securities) (Public Offers, Listing and Disclosures) Regulations, 2023.
The Board acknowledged that passenger demand across the aviation sector remains robust, but said external pressures have continued to weigh heavily on the airline's performance.

Fuel costs at Kenya Airways jumped 72% in the first half of 2026, with acting CEO George Kamal stating that fuel now represents up to 50% of total operating costs.

The International Air Transport Association projects jet fuel will average USD 152 (approximately KSh 19,600) per barrel in 2026, nearly 70% above the 2025 average of USD 90 (approximately KSh 11,600).
African carriers face an additional burden, paying around 17% more than the global average owing to limited local refining capacity, transport costs, and taxation.
The Middle East conflict has also forced airlines to reroute flights around affected airspace, stretching journey times and burning more fuel on connections between Africa, Europe, and Asia.

Kenya Airways did attract additional passengers redirected away from Gulf transit hubs, with load factors reaching as high as 99% on select routes, but the sharp rise in operating costs offset much of that revenue gain.
Trump announces fresh tariffs on 14 countries after Supreme Court ruling

The 2026 warning builds on a troubled recent history. In 2025, the airline posted a net loss of KSh 17.2 billion, reversing a net profit of KSh 5.4 billion recorded in 2024, which had been the carrier's first annual profit in over a decade.
Total income fell to KSh 161.5 billion in 2025, down from KSh 188.5 billion the previous year.

Much of that decline stemmed from the temporary grounding of three Boeing 787-8 Dreamliner aircraft due to supply chain difficulties, which cut capacity by 18% and reduced passenger numbers by roughly 13%.

The first half of 2026 showed no meaningful recovery. Although revenue grew 9% to KSh 81 billion, the airline still posted a loss after tax of KSh 16.1 billion, compared to KSh 12.2 billion over the same period in 2025.

Finance costs climbed 11.1% to KSh 12.4 billion, the basic loss per share reached KSh 2.94, and negative equity widened to KSh 132.1 billion from KSh 118.3 billion, with total liabilities rising 6% to KSh 315.3 billion.

Looking ahead to 2027, the airline said it would prioritise restoring its full fleet, reducing costs, conserving cash, and completing a capital-raising exercise designed to stabilise its balance sheet and support long-term growth.

items.title: Absa Bank Kenya Reports Kshs. 15.3 Billion Profit After Tax for Nine Months to September 2026
items.description: Absa Bank Kenya PLC recorded a return on equity of 19.9%, reflecting continued business resilience and the execution of its customer-focused growth strategy
content: Absa Bank Kenya PLC has reported a profit after tax of Kshs. 15.3 billion for the nine months ended September 30, 2026, supported by growth in customer lending, deposits and total assets, alongside strong capital and liquidity positions.
Absa Bank Kenya PLC recorded a return on equity of 19.9%, reflecting continued business resilience and the execution of its customer-focused growth strategy amid a lower interest rate environment.
According to its nine-month financial performance, customer assets grew by 11% to Kshs. 342.5 billion, while customer deposits increased by 6% to Kshs. 408 billion.

Total assets rose by 9% to Kshs. 604.1 billion, crossing the Kshs. 600 billion milestone for the first time and strengthening the bank’s capacity to finance businesses, households and key sectors of the Kenyan economy.
The growth in customer financing reflects increased support for individuals, entrepreneurs and businesses seeking capital to invest, expand operations and achieve their financial ambitions.
Customer deposits also increased, highlighting continued confidence in Absa Bank Kenya as a financial partner and the growing relevance of its banking solutions.
The bank said its balance sheet expansion was driven by deeper customer relationships and increased access to financial services.
Absa Bank Kenya posts Sh10.5 billion half-year profit
Absa Bank Kenya generated total revenue of Kshs. 44.7 billion during the nine-month period, supported by balance sheet growth and disciplined management of funding costs.
Net interest income stood at Kshs. 32.3 billion, recording growth in each successive quarter, while non-interest income contributed Kshs. 12.4 billion.
The bank said its third quarter delivered its strongest revenue performance of 2026, reflecting sustained business momentum despite the lower interest rate environment.

Commenting on the results, Absa Bank Kenya Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer Yusuf Omari said the performance demonstrated customer confidence and the strength of relationships built across the bank’s franchise.

“Our nine-month performance reflects the trust that customers continue to place in Absa and the strength of the relationships we have built across our franchise. In a lower interest rate environment, we remained focused on supporting our customers’ ambitions through accessible financing, innovative solutions and seamless banking experiences,” said Omari.
He added that the customer-led approach supported growth in both lending and deposits, with momentum building throughout the year.
The bank continued to strengthen its portfolio quality while maintaining disciplined cost management and investing in technology, talent and business transformation.
Its cost-to-income ratio closed at 42%, remaining within the bank’s strategic plan.
Asset quality also improved, with the non-performing loans (NPL) ratio declining to 9.8%, which the bank said remained below industry levels.
The loan loss ratio improved to 2.0%, reflecting better portfolio performance and effective risk management.
Absa Bank Kenya’s capital adequacy ratio stood at 19.3%, while liquidity reserves were maintained at 44.7%, providing a strong financial position to support future lending and business growth.
The bank’s return on equity of 19.9% also demonstrated its continued ability to generate value for shareholders.
Absa commits Shs230M to new global multi-asset investment fund
Digital transformation remained a key pillar of Absa Bank Kenya’s growth strategy during the reporting period.
One of the notable developments was the launch of Absa Next , described by the bank as Kenya’s first integrated digital financial ecosystem.
The platform brings together banking, savings, investments, credit and lifestyle services in one digital environment accessible to both Absa customers and non-customers.
The initiative is designed to simplify access to financial services while providing customers with a more integrated experience beyond traditional banking.

Absa also expanded its affluent banking proposition through the introduction of Kenya’s first co-branded travel and lifestyle credit card, extending customer benefits into travel and lifestyle services.
Absa Asset Management Limited strengthened its investment offering through the launch of two new Global Multi-Asset Special Funds.
The funds are denominated in Kenya shillings and US dollars, providing investors with additional investment options and opportunities to diversify their portfolios.
The launches form part of the wider group’s strategy to deepen customer engagement, strengthen its investment management business and diversify revenue streams.
Co-op Bank Q3 net profit hits Sh27.4bn; interim dividend rises 50pc
Strategic partnerships continued to play an important role in expanding Absa’s financial and non-financial solutions.
The bank said its collaborations enabled it to provide tailored solutions that respond to the changing needs of customers while supporting business development and economic inclusion.
In Kenya, Absa facilitated financing for solar-powered cold storage solutions aimed at addressing gaps in the agricultural value chain and reducing post-harvest losses.
The initiative seeks to strengthen agricultural productivity by improving storage infrastructure and helping farmers and other value-chain players preserve their produce.

The bank also supported the third edition of a hackathon in Kenya through an established partnership, providing a platform for young women to develop technology-driven solutions to practical challenges.
These initiatives demonstrate the bank’s continued focus on using financial services and strategic partnerships to promote innovation, sustainability and inclusive economic growth.
Absa Bank Kenya said it would continue investing in digital platforms, strategic partnerships and customer relationships as it pursues its ambition of becoming the financial partner of choice.

The bank’s strategy is anchored on its purpose of Empowering Africa’s tomorrow, together… one story at a time , with a focus on delivering customer-led innovation and sustainable value for customers, communities and shareholders.

“As we execute the next phase of our strategy, our ambition remains clear on being the financial partner of choice by delivering customer-led innovation, market-leading solutions and sustainable growth across all our businesses,” said Omari.
He noted that the bank’s strong capital position, expanding digital ecosystem and diversified franchise provided a solid foundation for capturing emerging opportunities and creating long-term value.

Absa Bank Kenya’s nine-month results highlight the resilience of its banking operations, supported by balance sheet expansion, improving asset quality, digital innovation and continued investment in Kenya’s economic development.

items.title: Former Kenyan Governor Jailed For Murder Of Varsity Student Pregnant With His Child
items.description: TVC News Nigeria is a 24-hour Nigeria-centric news, current affairs and documentary channel. The channel provides real-time, reliable and accurate news to Nigerians...
content: A former governor in Kenya has been sentenced to 25 years in prison for his role in the murder of a 26-year-old university student who was seven months pregnant with his child. The BBC reported that the High Court on Friday handed down the sentence to Zacharia Okoth Obado, former…...
A former governor in Kenya has been sentenced to 25 years in prison for his role in the murder of a 26-year-old university student who was seven months pregnant with his child.

The BBC reported that the High Court on Friday handed down the sentence to Zacharia Okoth Obado, former governor of Migori County, alongside two former aides, over the 2018 killing of Sharon Belyne Otieno.
The court established that Obado and Otieno had been involved in an “intimate relationship” which “subsequently led to a pregnancy with the deceased that the governor was unhappy about”.
Obado’s former personal assistant, Michael Oyamo, was also sentenced to 25 years in prison, while former county clerk Caspal Ojwang’ Obiero received an 18-year jail term.

In its findings, the court held that Obado supplied the motive and financial resources for the murder, while Oyamo coordinated its execution and Obiero provided logistical support and assisted in concealing the crime.
Presiding judge Cecilia Githua said Obado’s absence from Migori County when the killing occurred did not remove his responsibility for the crime.
The judge rejected the prosecution’s request for the death penalty, as well as Obado’s plea for a non-custodial sentence.
Otieno was killed between September 3 and 4, 2018, after leaving a hotel in Rongo, south-western Kenya, with journalist Barrack Oduor.
She had contacted Oduor to discuss her relationship with Obado, who was governor at the time. The pair were abducted shortly afterwards.
Oduor escaped by jumping out of a moving vehicle, and his account of the incident provided investigators with a crucial lead.
Otieno’s body was subsequently discovered near Kodera Forest. A post-mortem examination established that she died from strangulation and excessive bleeding caused by multiple stab wounds.
The court also confirmed that Obado was the biological father of Otieno’s unborn child.
Obado and his co-defendants were convicted of murder on July 23, 2026, after a lengthy trial during which prosecutors presented 42 witnesses and 81 exhibits.
However, the court declined to award compensation to Otieno’s family, ruling that there was insufficient evidence to establish the financial losses they had claimed.

Before the sentencing, Otieno’s mother appealed to the judge not to send Obado to prison, describing his imprisonment as “another death in the family”.
She urged the court to consider a non-custodial punishment, arguing that Otieno’s three children, from different relationships, needed his support.
Judge Githua, however, maintained that the family’s circumstances could not take precedence over the court’s responsibility to impose an appropriate punishment.
The family, through their lawyer, Antony Opondo, told Kenya’s Daily Nation that they would appeal the conviction, seeking Obado’s acquittal.
Otieno’s murder triggered protests and renewed public discussions about violence against women in Kenya.
A national survey found that at least 34 per cent of women had experienced physical violence in 2022.
The case has also attracted attention because criminal trials involving politicians of Obado’s stature are relatively rare in Kenya.

Obado served two terms as governor of Migori County in western Kenya. He initially moved between a smaller political party and the region’s dominant opposition movement before backing President William Ruto.
He formally joined Ruto’s ruling party in 2023 and became a regional organiser.
Both Obado’s legal team and those representing Otieno said they would appeal against the court’s decision.

items.title: KENYAN EX-GOVERNOR OBADO SENTENCED TO 25 YEARS FOR PREGNANT STUDENT’S MURDER

content: The High Court also handed prison terms to two former aides of the governor

A former governor of Migori County in Kenya, Zacharia Okoth Obado, has been sentenced to 25 years’ imprisonment for his role in the murder of 26-year-old university student Sharon Belyne Otieno, who was seven months pregnant with his child.

The High Court also handed prison terms to two former aides of the governor over the September 2018 killing. Michael Oyamo, Obado’s former personal assistant, was sentenced to 25 years, while former county clerk Caspal Ojwang’ Obiero received an 18-year jail term.

According to the court’s findings, Obado provided the motive and financial resources for the murder, Oyamo coordinated the operation, while Obiero assisted with logistics and efforts to conceal the crime.
Delivering the judgment, Justice Cecilia Githua maintained that Obado’s absence from Migori County at the time of the killing did not remove his responsibility for the crime.
The judge rejected the prosecution’s request for the death penalty and also dismissed Obado’s appeal for a non-custodial sentence.

Evidence presented during the trial established that Obado and Otieno were involved in an intimate relationship which resulted in her pregnancy. The court further established through evidence that the former governor was the biological father of the unborn child.
Otieno was murdered between September 3 and 4, 2018, after leaving a hotel in Rongo, southwestern Kenya, alongside journalist Barrack Oduor.
Reports indicated that Otieno had contacted Oduor to discuss her relationship with the then-governor. However, the two were abducted shortly after leaving the hotel.

Oduor managed to escape by jumping out of the moving vehicle in which they were being transported. His account of the incident subsequently provided investigators with a crucial lead, while Otieno’s body was later recovered near Kodera Forest.
A post-mortem examination revealed that she died from strangulation and severe blood loss resulting from multiple stab wounds.
Obado and his co-defendants were convicted of murder on July 23, 2026, following a prolonged trial during which the prosecution presented 42 witnesses and 81 exhibits to establish their involvement.
Before the sentencing, Otieno’s mother appealed to the court to spare Obado a prison term, arguing that his incarceration would amount to another loss for the family.
She requested a non-custodial sentence, explaining that Otieno’s three children, from different relationships, required his financial and parental support.
However, Justice Githua held that the family’s circumstances could not outweigh the need to impose an appropriate punishment for the offence.
The court also declined to grant the family compensation, citing insufficient evidence to substantiate the financial losses presented.

Meanwhile, the family, through its lawyer, Antony Opondo, told Kenya’s Daily Nation that it intended to appeal the judgment, seeking Obado’s acquittal. The legal teams representing the former governor and his co-defendants also indicated plans to challenge their respective sentences.
The killing generated widespread outrage in Kenya, sparking protests and renewed discussions about violence against women and the accountability of influential political figures.
The case also drew considerable public attention because prosecutions involving senior political figures are relatively uncommon in the country.

Obado served two terms as governor of Migori County in western Kenya. Throughout his political career, he moved between political parties before eventually aligning with President William Ruto’s administration.
He formally joined Ruto’s ruling party in 2023 and later became a regional organiser.
His sentencing brings a significant development in a murder case that has remained before the courts for years since Otieno’s death in 2018.

items.title: Kenya Met Predicts Dry Spell in Most Counties on Saturday, November 28, Lists Areas to Receive Rain
items.description: Kenya Met has forecast largely dry weather across most counties, listing areas expected to receive light rainfall and thunderstorms on Saturday, November 28

The Kenya Meteorological Service Authority has forecast largely dry weather across most parts of the country, with only a few counties expected to receive light rainfall and isolated thunderstorms on Saturday, November 28.

In its daily weather forecast issued on Friday, November 27, the department indicated that most counties would experience partly cloudy conditions at night, followed by sunny intervals in the morning and afternoon.
The outlook could concern farmers in areas relying on seasonal rainfall for crop production, particularly those whose agricultural activities depend on consistent precipitation.
However, the department did not issue a prolonged dry spell or drought warning, but indicated that rainfall would remain limited to a few locations.

According to the forecast, light showers and thunderstorms are expected in parts of the Coast, Eastern and Central regions.
In the Coast region, Mombasa, Kilifi, Tana River and Taita Taveta are among the counties likely to receive some rainfall. Kwale could also experience isolated light showers in the morning.

In the Eastern region, Marsabit, Meru, Tharaka-Nithi, Embu, Kitui, Machakos and Makueni are expected to receive varying amounts of light rainfall, with some areas likely to experience thunderstorms in the afternoon.
Murang'a and Kiambu are also expected to receive light showers and thunderstorms in a few places during the afternoon.
Kakamega is forecast to experience isolated showers and thunderstorms at night, although sunny intervals are expected during the day.
The rest of the counties, including Nairobi, Uasin Gishu, Nakuru, Kisumu , Busia, Siaya, Kericho, Bomet and Trans Nzoia, are expected to experience mainly sunny intervals.
Kenya Met forecasts rainfall in 39 counties from November 26 to December 3
Besides the rainfall outlook, the department warned of strong southerly to southeasterly winds exceeding 25 knots (12.5 metres per second) in parts of Marsabit and Turkana counties.
Residents in the affected areas should take precautions against the potentially disruptive winds.

The forecast also showed significant temperature variations across the country. Mandera is expected to record one of the highest maximum temperatures at 36°C, alongside Tana River and Turkana, which will experience similarly hot conditions.
On the other hand, Nyandarua is expected to record a minimum temperature of 11°C, making it one of the coldest counties during the forecast period.
Uasin Gishu, Narok and Kericho are expected to record minimum temperatures of 12°C. The forecast is valid from 9pm on Friday, November 27, to 9pm on Saturday, November 28.

items.title: Okoth Obado: Ex-Kenyan governor jailed for 25 years for killing pregnant girlfriend
items.description: The pregnant student was murdered after leaving a hotel with a journalist she had contacted to discuss her affair with the governor.
content: A former Kenyan governor has been jailed for 25 years for the murder of a university student who was seven months pregnant with his child.
The High Court on Friday sentenced Zacharia Okoth Obado, the former governor of Migori County, along with two former aides, over the 2018 killing of Sharon Belyne Otieno.
The investigation established that an "intimate relationship" had existed between Obado and Otieno, which "subsequently led to a pregnancy with the deceased that the governor was unhappy about".
Both Obado and Otieno's legal teams said they would appeal against the sentence.
His former personal assistant, Michael Oyamo, was also sentenced to 25 years in prison, while former county clerk Caspal Ojwang' Obiero received an 18-year sentence.
The court found that Obado had provided the motive and financial resources for the murder, while Oyamo coordinated its execution and Obiero provided logistical support and helped conceal the crime.
Judge Cecilia Githua said Obado's absence from Migori at the time of the killing did not absolve him of responsibility.
She rejected the prosecution's request for the death penalty, as well as Obado's plea for a non-custodial sentence.
Otieno, 26, was killed between 3 and 4 September 2018 after leaving a hotel in Rongo, south-western Kenya, with journalist Barrack Oduor.
She had contacted Oduor to discuss her relationship with the then-governor. The two were abducted shortly afterwards.
Oduor managed to escape by jumping out of a moving vehicle. His account of the abduction became a crucial lead in the investigation.
Otieno's body was later found near Kodera Forest.
A post-mortem examination found that she had died from strangulation and excessive bleeding caused by multiple stab wounds.
The court also established that Obado was the biological father of her unborn child.
Obado and his co-accused were convicted of murder on 23 July 2026, following a lengthy trial in which prosecutors called 42 witnesses and presented 81 exhibits.
On Friday, the court declined to award compensation to Otieno's family, saying there was insufficient evidence to establish the financial losses they had claimed.
Before sentencing, Otieno's mother had appealed to the judge not to send Obado to prison, saying his imprisonment would amount to "another death in the family".
She urged the court to consider a non-custodial sentence, arguing that Otieno's three children, from different relationships, needed his support.
But the judge said the family's circumstances could not override the court's responsibility to impose an appropriate punishment.
Otieno's family, through their lawyer Antony Opondo, told Kenya's Daily Nation that they would file an appeal seeking Obado's acquittal.
Otieno's murder sparked protests and renewed public debate about violence against women in Kenya.
A national survey found that at least 34% of women had experienced physical violence in 2022.
The case has also drawn attention because it is rare for such senior political figures to face public criminal trials in Kenya.
Obado served two terms as governor of Migori County in western Kenya, switching allegiance between a smaller political party and the region's dominant opposition movement.
He later backed President William Ruto and formally joined his ruling party in 2023, becoming a regional organiser.

items.title: Okoth Obado Case: Sharon’s Family to Appeal 25-Year Sentence, Wants Former Governor Freed
items.description: Sharon Otieno's family plans to appeal Okoth Obado's 25-year sentence for her murder, seeking his acquittal as his lawyers also prepare an appeal.

The family of slain university student Sharon Otieno plans to appeal the 25-year prison sentence handed to former Migori Governor Okoth Obado for her murder, seeking to have him acquitted.
The family's lawyer, Anthony Opondo, confirmed that they intend to challenge the sentence, which was delivered by the High Court in Milimani on Friday, November 27, 2026.
Obado's legal team has also announced plans to file a separate appeal against the decision, setting the stage for further legal proceedings in the high-profile murder case.

The family's decision comes after Justice Cecilia Githua sentenced Obado to 25 years in prison for the September 2018 murder of Sharon, a second-year Rongo University student who was seven months pregnant at the time of her death. A DNA test subsequently confirmed that Obado was the father of the unborn child.

The court also handed Obado's former personal assistant, Michael Juma Oyamo, a 25-year prison sentence, while former Migori County employee Caspal Ojwang Obiero was sentenced to 18 years for their roles in the killing.
The sentencing followed a judgment delivered on July 23, in which Justice Githua found all three men guilty of murder after considering evidence from 42 prosecution witnesses and 81 exhibits.
Okoth Obado sentenced to 25 years in prison over murder of Sharon Otieno
During sentencing, Justice Githua described Obado as the principal architect of the murder, saying he provided the motive, money and instructions that facilitated the killing.
She said Oyamo coordinated the murder while Obiero offered logistical support.

Before sentencing, Sharon's parents made an emotional appeal, asking the court to consider a non-custodial sentence for Obado. They said the former governor's family had approached them seeking reconciliation and that they had forgiven him.

Sharon's mother, Melinda Auma Rangili, told the court that her daughter's three children needed financial support and that allowing Obado to serve a non-custodial sentence would give him an opportunity to help provide for them.

She added that sentencing him to death or life imprisonment would feel like experiencing another death in her family. Sharon's father, Douglas Zakaria Otieno, also accepted reconciliation with Obado's family but expressed anger towards Oyamo and Obiero.
The court further declined to award compensation or restitution to Sharon's family, saying there was insufficient evidence to determine the losses they had presented.

items.title: Kenya, Zimbabwe strengthen bilateral ties through media cooperation
items.description: Kenya, Zimbabwe strengthen bilateral ties through media cooperation Kenya News Agency
content: Kenya and Zimbabwe have formalised cooperation in the media and information sector following the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between Kenya News Agency (KNA) and Zimbabwe’s Inter-African News Agency (NEW ZIANA).

The MoU was signed at State House, Nairobi, by Kenya’s Principal Secretary for Broadcasting and Telecommunications, Stephen Isaboke, and Zimbabwe’s Permanent Secretary for Information, Publicity and Broadcasting Services, Nick Ndabaningi Mangwana.
The signing follows Zimbabwean President Dr Emmerson Dambudzo Mnangagwa’s state visit to Kenya, where he held bilateral talks with President William Ruto at State House.

Speaking during the engagement, PS Isaboke said the MoU seeks to strengthen media cooperation between the two countries through enhanced collaboration, information sharing and professional engagement.

“As part of this engagement, I signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between the Kenya News Agency (KNA) and the Zimbabwe Inter-African News Agency (NEW ZIANA), alongside my Zimbabwean counterpart, the Permanent Secretary for Information, Publicity and Broadcasting Services, Mr Nick Ndavaningi Mangwana,” the PS said.
He revealed that the signing formed part of the broader bilateral engagements aimed at deepening cooperation and formalising agreements of mutual interest between the two countries.
“Today, I participated in the Kenya–Zimbabwe bilateral meeting held during the State Visit of President Emmerson Dambudzo Mnangagwa of Zimbabwe, hosted by President Dr William Ruto,” he said.

PS Isaboke said the MoU will provide a framework for the exchange of news and multimedia content, professional capacity building, sharing of knowledge and technical expertise, as well as collaboration in journalism and Information and Communication Technology (ICT).

“The MoU will provide a framework for the exchange of news and multimedia content, professional capacity building, sharing of knowledge and technical expertise, as well as collaboration in journalism and Information and Communication Technology (ICT),” he explained.

The MoU will pave the way for a stronger partnership between the two national news agencies, further enhancing institutional collaboration, promoting information sharing and facilitating the exchange of professional knowledge and expertise.
Isaboke added that the MoU will also promote people-to-people relations and enhance the visibility of African perspectives on regional and international media platforms.

The PS also underscored the importance of intra-African media cooperation in empowering African countries to tell their own stories, shape their narratives and showcase the continent’s development, innovation, cultural diversity and economic opportunities.

Isaboke revealed that the partnership will provide the Kenya News Agency (KNA) with an opportunity to strengthen its regional media presence, expand content exchange with NEW ZIANA and enhance the coverage and sharing of African stories across regional and international media platforms.

The partnership will also enhance information exchange between KNA and NEW ZIANA, promote the sharing of accurate and credible information, and strengthen the dissemination of African stories across regional and international media platforms.

“This partnership is an important step towards strengthening media cooperation, enhancing the flow of credible information and deepening the longstanding friendship between Kenya and Zimbabwe,” he said.
Established in 1963, the Kenya News Agency (KNA) is the government’s flagship news agency under the Directorate of Information, State Department for Broadcasting and Telecommunications.

The Agency plays a vital role in gathering, processing and disseminating credible, accurate and timely news and information to support national development and enable the public to make informed decisions.

With a presence in all 47 counties and 25 sub-county offices, KNA is strategically positioned to leverage the partnership to expand its reach, strengthen its visibility and enhance the sharing of Kenyan stories with regional and international audiences.

The collaboration with NEW ZIANA is expected to complement KNA’s mandate by creating opportunities for enhanced content exchange and professional collaboration and, more so, promote dissemination of credible African perspectives and news on the global media stage.
It will further contribute to the growth of Africa’s information ecosystem and advance the broader aspirations of continental integration.

items.title: Kenya Needs Its Own AI Models, Data Centres And Energy, Ndemo Says
items.description: The former ambassador argues that locally trained models, built around African languages and contexts, are essential to protecting data, expanding access and creating jobs.
content: Kenya must build its own artificial intelligence infrastructure and train models in local languages if it is to retain control of its data, develop relevant AI applications and capture more economic value from the technology, Dr Bitange Ndemo has said.

Speaking during a session on Sovereign AI at the CIO100 Symposium & Awards 2026 in Diani, the former Ambassador to Belgium and the European Union argued that relying on foreign AI models exposes African countries to external decisions over access, data and the technologies their economies increasingly depend on.
“Everybody can actually make their own AI which understands the local context,” Ndemo said, arguing that models must be trained to understand local laws, cultures and languages.

He described AI as a child’s brain that needs to be trained and shaped by its environment. A model developed elsewhere, he argued, may not adequately understand the differences between Kenyan, Tanzanian and Ugandan law, or the social and cultural contexts in which people use technology.

For Ndemo, sovereignty goes beyond hosting data locally. It requires countries to develop the supporting infrastructure, including data centres, reliable energy, connectivity, skilled engineers and locally trained language models.
Local languages are central to AI adoption
Ndemo said the limitations of foreign models become particularly significant when AI is expected to address problems rooted in local economic and social realities.

He argued that African languages do not always have direct equivalents for concepts such as data, productivity and predictability. Without the vocabulary to communicate these ideas accurately, he said, AI systems risk reproducing gaps in how development challenges are understood and addressed.
He used poverty as an example, arguing that efforts to address it have often failed to communicate the practical knowledge people need to improve their livelihoods.

In agriculture, he said, farmers need information that helps them use fewer resources to produce more. Locally trained models could help communicate such knowledge in languages and contexts that communities understand.

Ndemo also pointed to education, arguing that learning in a familiar language can improve comprehension. Personalised AI, he said, could adapt how information is delivered to an individual’s pace of understanding, potentially reaching learners who struggle in conventional classroom settings.

He said locally developed models could also help bridge the gap between formal education and practical knowledge, using the example of rural builders who understand roof angles through experience even when they may not connect that knowledge to classroom mathematics.
Sovereignty requires infrastructure and energy
Ndemo warned that dependence on foreign AI providers creates strategic risks for countries that lack control over the models they use.

He raised the possibility of an external provider restricting access to its services following a political or commercial decision, leaving businesses and public institutions without systems on which they have come to rely.
He also questioned the value African countries receive when they provide data that can be used elsewhere to develop commercial products, including medicines.
His argument was that African countries should retain greater control over the data and infrastructure needed to develop their own AI capabilities.

Energy, he said, is a critical part of that ambition. He urged African governments and investors to direct more capital towards electricity generation, arguing that data centres and GPU infrastructure require reliable and affordable power.

Citing Ethiopia’s investments in electricity generation, Ndemo said the country had moved ahead with large-scale energy projects that could support industrial activity and emerging technology industries.
He argued that Kenya should use available land and energy resources to attract infrastructure investment, create employment and support a growing cloud economy.
Building a talent pipeline and local AI industry
Ndemo said sovereign AI would also require sustained investment in engineers and other technical professionals who can build, train and maintain local systems.

He argued that developing local language models could create opportunities for African startups, content creators and technology businesses, while allowing countries to address challenges that imported systems may not adequately understand.

Among the potential applications he cited was healthcare. He described the use of smartphone-based tools to help health workers identify possible tuberculosis cases, illustrating how AI could support earlier diagnosis and intervention.
He also said locally developed systems could help create jobs by enabling businesses to build products and services around models trained for African markets.
Ndemo disclosed that he was working towards developing a Kenyan AI model and was seeking local partners willing to test and support the initiative before wider commercial participation.

He said the intention was to make a basic model available for people to begin using, with a broader national AI service offering that could support developers and businesses. He invited interested organisations to engage with the initiative, including through potential subscriptions to solutions built on the model.

His message to technology leaders was that AI sovereignty should not be reduced to a debate about foreign versus local software. It should be treated as a national capability involving energy, infrastructure, data, skills and language.
“Everything needed already exists. Only the model is missing,” Ndemo said.

items.description: More than 1,000 delegates from 80 countries have converged at Olkaria in Naivasha for the 3rd Annual Sustainable Energy Conference to discuss progress in green energy development and explore opportunities to address existing gaps in the sector.
content: More than 1,000 delegates from 80 countries have converged at Olkaria in Naivasha for the 3rd Annual Sustainable Energy Conference to discuss progress in green energy development and explore opportunities to address existing gaps in the sector.

The three-day conference, themed Powering Africa in the Green Industrial Revolution, has brought together stakeholders from the energy, finance, government and private sectors to explore investment opportunities and partnerships aimed at accelerating the transition to sustainable energy.

Speaking during the conference, KenGen CEO Engineer Peter Jenga said the company has identified several potential renewable energy projects currently undergoing feasibility studies, which are expected to inject additional megawatts into the national grid.
Jenga said the projects include a 42.5-megawatt solar power plant, an 8.6-megawatt Gogo hydroelectric power project and an 80.3-megawatt geothermal power plant.

“We have already completed the assessment of EPC contractors for a 42.5-megawatt solar power plant. We are also completing the assessment for the Gogo hydro power plant, which will generate 8.6 megawatts,” said Jenga.
He added that the company is exploring small hydro-power opportunities across the country to address challenges associated with reliance on conventional hydro-power generation.
One of the identified sites is in Webuye, where preliminary assessments indicate the potential to generate 26 megawatts of electricity.

The company is also considering wind energy development in Marsabit, which Jenga says has the potential to generate approximately 1,000 megawatts, with an initial 200-megawatt project being considered.
Meanwhile, Canada has reaffirmed its commitment to supporting Kenya’s energy transition through investment, technical cooperation and technology transfer.
Canadian High Commission Head of Cooperation Sophie Grace said Canada is keen to explore opportunities in Kenya’s energy sector, including nuclear energy and drilling technologies.
She noted that Canada’s extensive experience in energy production could help Kenya strengthen its capacity and position itself as a regional energy exporter.
“We would really like to help support Kenya to move into becoming a large exporter in the region, and that is one of our goals in this collaboration,” said Grace.

Energy and Petroleum Regulatory Authority (EPRA) Director of Economic Regulation and Strategy Dr John Mutua called for stronger public-private partnerships to mobilise investments and accelerate the implementation of viable energy projects.
Mutua said collaboration with private investors remains critical in achieving Kenya’s energy transition while ensuring consumer protection and sustainability in the sector.

“As we work towards energy transition and ensuring that Kenya is powered with renewable energy, we hope to match the needs of investors while protecting consumers and ensuring a sustainable energy sector,” he said.

The discussions come as Kenya pursues its ambition of transitioning to a predominantly renewable energy-powered economy by 2034, with strategic partnerships, increased investment and technology transfer expected to play a central role in achieving the target.

The three-day conference is expected to provide a platform for stakeholders to strengthen international cooperation, identify investment opportunities and develop strategies to accelerate Africa’s green industrial revolution.
