items.title: Organisation takes anti-GBV campaign to communities affected by violence
items.description: Organisation takes anti-GBV campaign to communities affected by violence Kenya News Agency
content: Youth for a Sustainable World (YSW) has joined community organisations, health officials, police officers and other partners in marking the launch of the 16 Days of Activism against gender-based violence (GBV), calling for community action, support for survivors and access to justice for victims.

Speaking during the launch at Mukuru kwa Njenga estate, Nairobi County, Christabel Were, a Projects Officer at YSW supporting programme implementation, said the event was organised to remember women and girls who have experienced violence, honour survivors and raise awareness about the need to end GBV.

Ms. Were said the choice of venue, located next to the Mukuru dumpsite, was deliberate, given the history of violence against women in the area, including the recovery of women’s bodies (suspected victims of femicide) from the dumpsite in July 2024.
She noted that the event provided an opportunity for the community to reflect on the experiences of victims and survivors while renewing its commitment to fighting violence against women and girls.
“Today is basically about remembering these women, celebrating them, but also calling the community to action,” she said.

According to Ms. Were, YSW has been working in Mukuru for several years, through organised youth groups and existing community structures to reach young people and promote awareness of gender-based violence and sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR).
The Projects Officer explained that the organisation works with peer educators aged between 10 and 24 years through its youth empowerment centres to reach young people within the community.
They also collaborate with community health promoters and sub-county health teams to mobilise residents, provide information and link survivors to essential support services.
Ms. Were emphasised the importance of strengthening partnerships with law enforcement agencies, particularly police gender desks, to ensure survivors receive assistance and can pursue justice.
She observed that while reporting and awareness efforts are important, access to justice remains a significant challenge for many survivors.
Through its initiatives, it seeks to support survivors to navigate through legal processes and be able to access justice.
“We want these survivors to get justice. The call is usually to support these survivors so that they are able to navigate the legal processes and actually get justice,” she said.

During this year’s 16 Days of Activism, YSW plans to intensify its awareness campaigns across the 13 counties where it operates through community events, webinars, digital platforms and partnerships with other stakeholders.
In Nairobi, the organisation has identified Embakasi South and Embakasi East as key areas of focus, with activities aimed at mobilising communities and strengthening the fight against GBV.
Ms. Were urged young people and community members to speak out against gender-based violence, support survivors and actively participate in efforts to prevent further cases.
She said ending GBV requires collective responsibility, noting that raising awareness and encouraging young people to use their voices can help trigger meaningful action.

“The power is usually in their hands. We need to rally young people to have that voice and urgency to speak about these issues. The more we speak about it, the more we bring awareness, and the more we can get action taken,” she said.

YSW called on communities, partners and relevant authorities to work together to ensure that survivors are supported, perpetrators are held accountable and women and girls can live free from violence.

Nyambura Kahanyah, the facility in-charge and Manager at Kware Dispensary, said most cases reported at the facility involve physical violence affecting both men and women, while sexual violence also accounts for a number of cases handled.
Ms Kahanyah said financial challenges were among the major factors forcing survivors, particularly women, to remain in abusive relationships.
She observed that some women continue living with abusive partners because they depend on them financially and lack alternative sources of income to support themselves and their families.

“For a woman to stay in a marriage that is not working and where she is being violated, sometimes it is because she does not have support from outside. She continues staying with the person violating her because of the financial support she receives,” she said.
The dispensary manager noted that economic empowerment initiatives were essential in helping survivors become financially independent and make informed decisions about their safety and future.
She said many cases of GBV go unreported because survivors fear the consequences of reporting individuals who provide for their household needs.
“So many cases are not reported. How do you report the person who is supporting you in the house?” she posed.
She explained that the facility handles basic medical services before referring survivors requiring specialised attention to higher-level facilities, including Tumaini Clinic in Mukuru.
Ms Kahanyah added that the survivors seeking to pursue legal action are also guided to the police station’s gender desk to facilitate reporting and access to relevant support services.

She emphasised the importance of coordination between healthcare providers and law enforcement agencies to ensure survivors receive appropriate medical attention, counselling and assistance in pursuing justice.

Ms Kahanyah commended the partnership between Kware Dispensary, Youth for a Sustainable World (YSW) and the Sisbro of Zion Foundation for supporting survivors, particularly those facing financial difficulties.

She said partners have been instrumental in providing transport assistance for survivors requiring referrals to health facilities, counselling, mentorship and follow-up for survivors, helping them recover and rebuild their lives.
Kahanyah called on the government to strengthen the capacity of police officers through specialised training on gender-based violence and the appropriate handling of survivors.
“Uniformed officers should be equipped with the skills to receive complaints sensitively, protect survivors’ dignity and guide them through the reporting and justice processes.”

Students urged to seek help amid concerns over teenage mental health
items.description: Students urged to seek help amid concerns over teenage mental health Kenya News Agency
content: High school students have been urged to speak out about mental health challenges and seek professional support amid growing concerns over teenage suicide and other forms of emotional distress.

Children officers from the State Department for Children Services cautioned learners against suffering in silence, urging them to seek guidance and counselling when confronted with stress, anxiety, peer pressure, low self-esteem and family-related challenges.

The officers spoke during an end-year mentorship conference at Enoomatasiani Girls High School in Kajiado North Sub-County, which brought together hundreds of Form Three students benefiting from the Jomo Kenyatta Foundation (JKF) Elimu Scholarship Programme.

Elizabeth Wawire, a Children Officer, said while scholarships had helped improve access to education for vulnerable learners, financial support alone was not sufficient to address the challenges they face.
She noted that some beneficiaries grapple with emotional and social difficulties that require mentorship, counselling and parental support.

Wawire said the mentorship programme, implemented in collaboration with JKF, provides an opportunity to equip learners with life skills, strengthen their resilience and guide them through challenges associated with adolescence.
She also called on parents and guardians to pay closer attention to their children’s emotional well-being, particularly during school holidays when learners spend more time at home.

Wawire urged parents to create supportive environments where teenagers can freely discuss their challenges without fear of judgement, adding that listening to children and monitoring changes in their behaviour were important in identifying distress early.

Another Children Officer, Billy Adera, challenged learners to exercise responsibility in their use of technology and social media, warning that online interactions could expose them to exploitation and harmful content.
He cited cases of young people whose lives had been adversely affected by negative online experiences, urging students to be cautious about the information they consume and share.

Adera also warned against online exploitation, including blackmail involving intimate images shared or obtained without consent. He encouraged learners facing online harassment, threats or any form of abuse to report the incidents instead of suffering in silence.
Adera also advised students to seek assistance through the Child Helpline toll-free number 116 or WhatsApp number 0722 116 116.

Ashley Merit, a student at Ruthimitu Girls High School who attended the conference, urged fellow learners to embrace positive behaviour, remain alert to challenges affecting their well-being and seek help whenever necessary.

“Change begins with you. We must be mindful of our character; watch out for the challenges we face and never be afraid to speak up whenever we encounter difficulties. There is help available, and we should not suffer in silence,” she said.
The conference underscored the importance of mentorship, guidance and counselling in helping adolescents navigate social and emotional pressures, build resilience and make responsible decisions.

items.title: Kenya Halves New HIV Infections as Child Treatment Lags
items.description: Kenya cut new HIV infections by 56.5 percent, yet 19,434 people died in 2025 as paediatric care lags and US donor transition looms toward 2030.
content: Kenya cut new HIV infections by 56.5 percent, yet 19,434 people died in 2025 as paediatric care lags and US donor transition looms toward 2030.

Kenya cut new HIV infections by 56.5 percent between 2021 and 2025, yet 19,434 people died of AIDS-related causes last year, exposing severe paediatric treatment gaps and rising financial strain as foreign donor support declines.

Ahead of World AIDS Day on December 1, National Syndemic Diseases Control Council (NSDCC) Chief Executive Officer Dr Douglas Bosire and National AIDS and STI Control Programme (NASCOP) head Dr Andrew Mulwa released the 2026 Kenya HIV Estimates. With about 1.4 million Kenyans living with HIV, the data show progress in adult care is masking stalled outcomes for children, youth, and men.

According to the NSDCC estimates, new infections dropped from 32,027 in 2021 to 13,936 in 2025, extending an 82 percent decline since 2015. Even so, the country still logs roughly 38 new infections and 53 preventable HIV-related deaths every day, meaning annual deaths now outnumber new cases by nearly 5,500.

Gender disparities also cut in opposite directions across diagnosis and survival. Women aged 15 and older accounted for 7,363 new infections in 2025, more than double the 3,177 recorded among adult men. Yet men represent nearly half of all HIV-related deaths because lower testing and delayed clinic enrolment leave many untreated until advanced illness.

Adolescents and young adults remain a major transmission driver. Young people aged 15 to 24 accounted for 4,322 new infections, or 41 percent of all adult cases, while children and youth under 25 together represented 55 percent of total new infections nationwide.

The widest gap sits in paediatric HIV care. While the 69,330 Kenyan children aged 14 and younger living with HIV make up 4.7 percent of the total HIV population, they accounted for 2,226 deaths in 2025, or 11.5 percent of national AIDS fatalities. Their AIDS mortality rate stands at 32.1 per 1,000, compared with 12.2 among adults.

NASCOP data show Kenya's paediatric care cascade stands at 79 percent diagnosed, 60 percent on antiretroviral therapy, and 52 percent virally suppressed, far behind the national average of 93, 91, and 87 percent and the global 95-95-95 target. Roughly 14,559 children remain undiagnosed, while 21,908 diagnosed children are not receiving treatment.

Mother-to-child transmission stood at 8.04 percent in 2025, above the global benchmark of under 5 percent. Bosire said 72 percent of the 3,396 new paediatric infections stemmed from pregnant women starting antenatal care late or taking medication inconsistently during pregnancy and breastfeeding, urging male partners to support attendance across four recommended clinic visits.

Sustaining treatment is growing financially harder. Bosire estimated Kenya spends between Sh15,000 and Sh20,000 per patient annually, putting the national drug and care bill at Sh20 billion to Sh25 billion a year. Development partners currently cover about 66 percent of national HIV spending compared with 34 percent from domestic budgets, and the United States expects Kenya to assume full financing by 2030.

Patients are already feeling external aid cuts. Between April and June 2026, supply disruptions left some clinics issuing one- or two-week antiretroviral refills instead of three-month prescriptions, raising transport costs and missed-dose risks.

A July 2026 amfAR survey found 73 percent of US-funded Kenyan groups had halted services for key populations such as sex workers, while The Star reported on November 26 that some HIV patients are now paying up to Sh2,000 for diagnostic tests once provided free.

NSDCC is opening World AIDS Day commemorations with a national half marathon at Nyayo National Stadium on November 29 before county-level medical camps and accountability forums on December 1. Alongside faith-sector partnerships targeting adolescent pregnancies and HIV under its Triple Threat campaign, health officials say closing paediatric diagnosis gaps and replacing donor funds in national and county budgets will decide whether recent gains hold.

As AIDS Healthcare Foundation Kenya Country Director Dr Samuel Kinyanjui noted, preventing child HIV deaths is now a test of logistics, clinic retention, and domestic financing rather than medical science.
